sentences.text: Sinornithosaurus is a genus of feathered dromaeosaurid dinosaur, a name that translates to 'Chinese bird-lizard'.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — measured 1.2 meters in length and weighed between 3 and 5 kilograms.
However, other descriptions note that the animal was among the smallest dromaeosaurids, with a length of about 90 centimeters.
This small predator possessed proportionally very long arms and hands.
Its body was covered in contour feathers generally between 3 and 4.5 centimeters long, composed of filaments showing characteristics of early feathers.
Sinornithosaurus holds the distinction of being the first dromaeosaurid dinosaur discovered with feathers.
It was the fifth non-avian feathered dinosaur genus discovered by 1999, a finding that caused a sensation in the scientific community.
Analysis of microscopic cell structures suggests the animal had black and rufous feathers.
A subsequent 2012 study showed that the colors included reddish-brown, yellow, black, and gray, which were scattered across its body.
The genus Sinornithosaurus was described by Xu, Wang, and Wu in 1999.
Xu Xing, Wang Xiaolin, and Wu Xiaochun of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology of Beijing discovered the fossils.
The type species Sinornithosaurus millenii was the one formally described in that year.
A second species, S. haoiana, meaning 'Chinese Hao bird-lizard', was described by Liu et al. in 2004 based on a specimen differing from S. millenii in head and hip characters.
The presence of feathers in Sinornithosaurus suggests that other running dromaeosaurids, such as Velociraptor, may also have possessed feathers.
Some scientists suggest Sinornithosaurus could have glided for short distances after leaping from trees.
Turner, Makovicky, and Norell concluded that specimen NGMC 91 was a subadult individual of Sinornithosaurus millenii.
Sinornithosaurus belonged to the family Dromaeosauridae, a group of agile predators known for having a distinctive sickle-shaped claw on their toes.
Phylogenetic analysis by Xu Xing demonstrated that Sinornithosaurus is basal or primitive among dromaeosaurs.
Xu Xing described Sinornithosaurus and presented a phylogenetic analysis demonstrating it is a basal, or primitive, dromaeosaurid.
The parent group of Sinornithosaurus is Microraptorinae.
Sinornithosaurus millenii lived approximately 125 million years ago during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, making it one of the earliest known dromaeosaurids.
Fossils of Sinornithosaurus haoiana and the specimen NGMC 91 date to approximately 122 million years ago.
Sinornithosaurus lived 125 million years ago during the Barremian (Early Cretaceous), making it one of the oldest and most primitive members of its family.
Sinornithosaurus lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.

Turner, Makovicky, and Norell (2012) argued that the distinguishing features of S. haoiana were either present in S. millenii or variable, leading them to consider S. haoiana a junior synonym of S. millenii.
However, Turner, Makovicky, and Norell in 2012 argued that the supposed distinctive features of S. haoiana are present in S. millenii or vary among Sinornithosaurus specimens.
In 2009, a team led by Empu Gong suggested Sinornithosaurus was the first identified venomous dinosaur based on grooved teeth and a possible venom gland cavity.
Longrich and Currie (2009) expressed the opinion that Sinornithosaurus was probably too heavy to fly.
In 2009, a team led by Enpu Gong examined a well-preserved skull and found evidence suggesting it is the first identified venomous dinosaur.
